entries.title: Replika
entries.intro: Replika is the AI companion, with 42 million users worldwide. In 2026, midway through a full rebrand under a new CEO, the company brought us in to lead design engineering: a flat team of twenty, working across iOS, web, brand, and the design system.
body: The brief was to define the flagship features of the product's next era. We carried each one from direction to spec to build, shipping directly with the lead iOS developer.

The harder question was what that era should be. The rebrand was live and the vision still in motion, so we did not start from features. We followed how people actually used the product, and the use pointed to one reframe: memory is the product. That call set the direction for everything after it.

Memory V2 grew into Portraits, Life Arcs, and People Cards, each built on structured memory drawn from conversation. Alongside it we shipped the 2026 design system grown from the brand book, a 40-screen onboarding recast as a six-act narrative, and the dual-currency economy through which users shape the relationship.

entries.title: Parable
entries.desc: An intelligence layer for the enterprise.
entries.intro: Parable is the intelligence layer for enterprise operations. It reads the whole company and surfaces where the work, the waste, and the automation hide.
body: In September 2025 the founders brought us in as their sole product designer. They had engineers on staff, no product director, and a loose direction. We gave it shape: an end-to-end journey for the ideal customer, prototyped first in Figma, then in code beside the front-end engineer.

The real problem was drift. The product had a visual language and no system beneath it, and every sprint widened the gap between what shipped and what cohered. For an AI to operate the product, taste had to become rules. Our audit cut the colour set from roughly 60 tokens to 18, spacing from 24 to 13, and chart tokens from more than 50 to 12, until a model could compose from a named space of valid output.

The hardest call was density. Our first attempt put a density prop on every component. It worked in isolation and fell apart in composition: a compact table inside a comfortable card had two sources of truth. We tore the prop out and moved density onto the DOM, one attribute on a container, resolved through the cascade. The prop was more flexible; the cascade was more composable, and in a system an AI recomposes, composability wins. We shipped that foundation, and the remaining budget moved to engineering to build from it.

details.label: Context
details.text: Enterprise UX is bad because the org chart leaks into the product. Every team ships its own UI dialect, so fragmented APIs become fragmented UX. Parable's bet is the opposite — composability as the future of software, with PMs and AI assembling experiences from shared building blocks rather than designers hand-drawing every flow. That only pays off if the blocks are real — and when this work opened, they weren't.

details.label: Problem
details.text: The inheritance was a visual language with no system beneath it — no token architecture, no component taxonomy, no progressive-disclosure model. With no designer on staff, engineering filled every gap ad-hoc, and each sprint widened the distance between what shipped and what cohered. The audit quantified the bloat — roughly two-thirds of the audited token categories, redundant: colour palettes 5→3 (~60→18 tokens), spacing 24→13, chart tokens 50+→12.

details.label: Approach
details.text: The fix: reframe the design language as a Shared Capability inside Parable's own maturity pipeline (dog food → Labs → Previews → Shared Capabilities), built on one severe principle — design intent that cannot be computed cannot be enforced. So the system is authored as a contract: structured layers (philosophy → principles → form → vocabulary → tokens → components → composition), machine-checkable in principle rather than dependent on a reviewer in the room, on an atomic ladder that tightens Labs → Preview → Stable.

details.label: Build
details.text: The system's hardest problem: Parable serves an executive who wants one conclusive number and an engineer who wants the full grouping — the same data at two densities. Cosmetic token systems answer "what colour / radius / spacing"; they have no word for "register-3, data-dense surface." So density became a first-class, decoupled axis — three tiers (Sparse / Comfortable / Compact) expressed as a contract, with hard whitespace floors: Executive ≥55%, Operational ≥40%, Configuration ≥35%.

details.label: System
details.text: The language is small enough to hold. The "Threshold" palette encodes the philosophy — light emerges from darkness: a dark field, content emerging through luminosity, one gradient reserved for action and rank, a serif display over a grotesque, one radius family. The audit's cut is what makes it enforceable — a token set small enough that an agent composes from a named space of valid output, not an open canvas.

details.label: Detail
details.text: One data-density attribute re-poses an entire screen. The same CX work report meets an executive at Sparse — one number, almost alone on the field — an operator at Comfortable — the charts beneath it — and a configurator at Compact — the controls. Density (whitespace, type scale, elevation) follows from the posture, never set by hand.

details.label: Iteration
details.text: The first attempt was the obvious one: a density prop on every component, threaded down through context. It worked in isolation and fell apart in composition — a compact table inside a comfortable card had two sources of truth. So density moved out of the component tree and onto the DOM: one data-density on a container, resolved through a CSS attribute cascade. The prop was more flexible; the cascade was more composable — and in a system an AI recomposes, composability wins.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: Ponder composes interfaces; ask an LLM for the same screen twice and you get two layouts. So the design system becomes the constraint layer that makes generated output trustworthy — an agent declares intent ("a register-3 report for an executive") and the system resolves architecture, posture, voice and density. The enforcement layer — a codegen pass and a constraint engine — is designed but deliberately not built: two shipped primitives earned more than a validator would at twenty people. Foundation shipped — the entropy cut that closes KPI 1, priority components built in sync. From visual language to Shared Capability.

entries.title: Mountains
entries.desc: A micro design system for a luxury technology house.
entries.intro: Mountains is a luxury technology house: a studio that builds for the luxury industry, and a fund that invests in it. We gave it a micro design system, small enough to hold in one hand, and one surface to prove it on.
body: The brief asked for a mountain in watercolour. Our first two builds followed every rule we had written and still read as vector art, because the rules described what a watercolour looks like, not what pigment does on paper.

We moved the painting into a WebGL shader. Shadow is not drawn: it is derived from the surface against a travelling sun, then laid down in a few wash bands. The faces that meet the sun are simply unpainted paper.

The system around it is deliberately small: one palette taken from the painting, two typefaces, one control height, one easing curve, and a mark built on a seven-row grid. Every square on this page is rendered by the landing's own code. The landing turns three moments, Mountains, Technology and Capital, on one canvas while the light moves beneath them.

rail.alt: The mark — a seven-row staircase in light inks, arriving square by square on the painting's sky.
The type — the statement in its two voices, pigment and sky, with its door beneath.
The painting — the massif rendered live, its shadow derived from a travelling sun and laid in wash bands.
The instrument — the segment control at poster scale, its glass thumb walking Mountains, Technology and Capital.
The construction — the mark addressed cell by cell on an eleven-by-eleven lattice.
The landing, in use — walking the three moments, opening a page and returning to the painting.
